A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has never seen.
Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the constraint must be enforced at inference time.
Enforcing it must not discard what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the obstacle yet fail the task.
We therefore want actions that are both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.

Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy’s running estimate of the clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it.
We instead build on rejection and projection.
Rejection redraws actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare.
Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is efficient, but the result need not be plausible.
Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection’s efficiency and rejection’s plausibility.

CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler, projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is safe.
Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs.

Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pickand-place, an orientation preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81% safe success on the shelf and 55% on hardware, against 55% and 40% for projection, while staying plausible.

Large-scale flow-matching and diffusion policies have become capable generalist priors for robot manipulation[1, 2]: trained once on broad demonstrations, a single model can pick and place objects, open drawers, and fold clothes.

Yet no training set anticipates every deployment, and such a policy will inevitably meet safety-critical scenarios its demonstrations never contained, for example: a wine glass left beside the drawer it must open, which the arm must not touch.
This requirement is a constraint, supplied only at deployment.
It defines a safe set: the set of actions that satisfy it; in our example, every action that does not touch the glass.
Our goal is to sample actions that both come from the policy and lie in the safe set, without retraining the policy for each new constraint.

The natural approach is to correct the policy’s output: sample an action and project it onto the safe set, moving it to the nearest safe action, or steer the denoising trajectory using a function of the constraint.
Such corrections address the second half of this goal, moving the action into the safe set.
They can lose the first: the correction can move the action somewhere the policy would rarely sample.
This matters because the policy is what captures the task.
An action it considers unlikely may clear the wine glass yet no longer reach the drawer handle.
Such an action also loses what the policy learned from the demonstrations, beyond the task itself: smooth, kinematically feasible motion.
We therefore require the sampled action to be both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.
10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA.

texts: Figure 1: Sampling a flow-matching policy under a deployment-time constraint.
Left: The policy πθ denoises Gaussian noise a₀ ∼ N (0, I) (t=0 → 1) into an action chunk a ∼ πθ , a short sequence of robot motions.
Its draws are multimodal: three ways to reach the apple, drawn as paths in the real scene and as modes of the density πθ (a); the most likely passes through the obstacle.
Middle: Constraints such as obstacle avoidance or velocity and joint limits, and soft costs L, are supplied only at deployment.
The obstacle constraint defines a safe set C, the actions that avoid it.

Right: We want actions that are safe (a ∈ C) and plausible (likely under πθ ), i.e. draws from πθ (a) 1C (a), where 1C is 1 on C and 0 elsewhere: the unsafe mode is removed and the others keep their shape.
CS-Pi (ours) targets this distribution without retraining the policy.
Among such training-free samplers, the most common is gradient guidance [3, 4, 5], which nudges each denoising step along the gradient of a cost on the action.
Guidance has two shortcomings.
First, safety constraints are typically hard constraints: an action either satisfies them or violates them, with no degree in between.
An action either touches the wine glass or it does not; this yesor-no answer says nothing about which way to move the arm, so a hard constraint offers no gradient to follow.
Guidance must instead use a smooth cost, such as a collision cost that grows as the arm nears the glass, which discourages contact but does not rule it out.
Second, even a smooth cost is meaningful only on a clean action, while guidance acts on noisy intermediate states.
Guidance therefore evaluates the cost at a proxy: the policy’s running estimate of the clean action, an average over every clean action the noisy state could still become.
This proxy is reliable only when the cost changes slowly across those actions, so sharpening the cost toward the true constraint makes guidance less reliable, not more.
The proxy fails when the policy is uncertain between distinct modes, such as passing left or right of the glass.
The average of the two can pass straight through the glass, an action the policy would never sample.
The gradient evaluated there may point towards neither mode (App.
We instead build on rejection and projection, two classical mechanisms that act only on the final sampled action rather than guiding the intermediate noise levels.
Rejection sampling redraws complete actions from the policy until one satisfies the constraint: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare.
Projection maps a sampled action to the nearest constraintsatisfying point: it is efficient, but the projected action need not be plausible and can be jerky or task-irrelevant.
Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection’s efficiency and rejection’s plausibility.

When a projected action is implausible, we need not take rejection’s drastic step of restarting sampling from pure noise; we can instead resample from a reduced noise level around the projection, so the policy returns a safe and plausible action near the projection.
We operationalize this insight in CS-Pi, a draw-project-renoise sampler (Fig. 2).
CS-Pi starts from a single draw from the policy and refines it in a loop.
Each iteration projects the current draw onto the safe set and, rather than executing the possibly implausible projection, adds noise back to it, scaled to how far the projection moved the draw.
It then re-runs the unmodified policy from that noise level to obtain the next draw.
The loop ends once a draw is safe.

texts: Figure 2: Sampling a safe action from a flow-matching policy.
Gradient guidance steers each denoising step with a cost gradient evaluated at a proxy and can still violate the constraint.
Projection moves the draw to the safe set, yielding an action the policy would rarely sample.
Rejection sampling redraws from pure noise until a draw is safe.
CS-Pi projects the draw, renoises the projection to time n = k/(k + δ) set by the projection residual δ (larger δ renoises more), and re-runs the policy until a draw is safe and plausible.

We first present CS-Pi for hard constraints, then extend it to continuous costs, such as an orientation preference, by replacing only the projection step.
The same change lets CS-Pi combine hard constraints with costs.

Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place with deployment-time obstacles, the orientation preference above, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi is the only sampler that satisfies the constraint while staying plausible wherever the constraint permits; on the shelf it reaches 81% safe success (completing the task without collision) against 55% for projection and 32% for gradient guidance.
Gradient guidance.

In the robotic settings we consider, constraints and preferences are typically expressed as analytic costs on the action, such as a signed-distance collision cost, a joint-limit penalty or an orientation error.

The standard way to steer a diffusion or flow-matching policy [6] toward low cost at deployment is gradient guidance, which nudges each denoising step along the gradient of that cost: classifier-free guidance [4, 7], DPS [8], ΠGDM [9], MPGD [10], AdjointDPM [11], Diffuser [3], and Lan-o3dp [12].
But the cost is meaningful only on a clean action, so each method evaluates it at a proxy, the policy’s running estimate of the clean action.
The proxy is accurate when the cost changes slowly and the policy has settled on one mode, and it breaks down otherwise, pushing the sample toward implausible actions (App.

Trust Sampling [13] takes several guidance steps per denoising step, capping their number by how far the proxy can be trusted at that noise level and stopping early when the sample leaves the region the policy was trained on.
It shares our aim of keeping samples plausible, but every step still follows the proxy’s gradient.
Rejection, reweighting, and projection.
A constraint can also be met without following the proxy’s gradient, by acting on the policy’s clean actions.
Rejection sampling redraws complete actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare.

Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers reweight and resample a population of particles rather than discarding them (the Twisted Diffusion Sampler [14], Feynman–Kac samplers [15, 16]); they need more particles as the safe set shrinks, and the weight that steers each particle at a noisy step is still evaluated at the proxy (App.

Projection moves a sample to the nearest safe action without any cost gradient, either at every denoising step [17] or once, on the final action, which is then executed; in both cases the projected action need not be plausible.

CS-Pi also avoids the proxy’s gradient but combines rejection and projection: it projects the final action, then renoises the projection rather than executing it and re-denoises it with the policy, returning a plausible draw closer to the safe set without rejection’s wait or SMC’s particle budget.

texts: Control-barrier-function samplers.

SafeDiffuser [18] enforces forward invariance by solving a control-barrier-function (CBF) quadratic program at each denoising step; SafeFlowMatcher [19] alternates flow prediction with barrier-based correction; and SAD-Flower [20] augments a flow with a virtual safe control input and a learned dynamics model.
These methods are designed to certify safety under their respective assumptions, but the certificate says nothing about plausibility.

Their corrections continuously deform the current sample: when a constraint blocks the mode the sample has committed to, a correction can push it out of the unsafe region but does not redraw it from another mode of the policy.
CS-Pi instead projects, renoises and re-denoises with the policy, which allows such a mode switch while keeping each draw plausible.
CBF samplers also require a differentiable barrier with the structure needed to evaluate its Lie derivatives and relative degree; SAD-Flower additionally assumes a learned dynamics model.
CS-Pi requires only a projection onto the safe set, which enables its zero-shot use with existing policies, such as π₀.₅, and obstacle bounding boxes estimated from vision (Sec. 4.4).
We test SafeDiffuser and SafeFlowMatcher on the same policies and report them in Tables 1 and 2 and App.
B. SAD- Flower is not evaluated as it requires a learned dynamics model, which our setups do not provide.
Deployment-time safety for vision-language-action models.
Recent work shares our practical motivation of enforcing constraints on a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy at deployment.
OmniGuide [5] steers flow-matching VLAs [2, 21] toward collision avoidance and semantic targets with gradient guidance on differentiable energy fields, and thus evaluates its cost at the proxy.

VLSA [22] instead acts once, on the final action, much as projection does: a CBF filter changes the VLA’s output action as little as possible to satisfy the barrier condition, and the robot executes the filtered action.
Its authors report that this filter causes a safety-induced distribution shift.
Our hardware experiment uses a similar setup, a π₀.₅ policy on a Franka arm, and there CS-Pi improves on both gradient guidance and projection (Sec. 4.4).
Partial renoising.
Adding noise to an input and denoising it again is an established way to make an edited input plausible under a generative model.

SDEDIT [23] renoises a user’s stroke painting and denoises it into a realistic image; REPAINT [24] renoises around known pixels to inpaint the rest; and DEMODIFFUSION [25] renoises a human demonstration retargeted to the robot into actions the policy would plausibly produce.
In each, the renoised input is given in advance and the amount of noise is set by hand, once.
CS-Pi instead renoises the policy’s own draw after projecting it onto the safe set, sets the amount of noise from how far the projection moved the draw, and repeats until a draw is safe.
This turns a one-shot edit into a loop that drives the draw toward the safe set (Sec. 3).
We want to sample from a flow-matching policy under a constraint supplied only at deployment time.
The action we draw must satisfy two equally important requirements: it must be safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.
An action the policy would essentially never draw, even one that satisfies the constraint, may be jerky, kinematically infeasible, or taskinappropriate.
Setup and notation.
The policy πθ generates a clean action a ∈ RD by integrating a learned velocity field along an ODE, from Gaussian noise a₀ ∼ N (0, I) at time t = 0 to the clean action at t = 1.

We write a = πθ (an; n) for integrating from an intermediate state an at time t = n ∈ [0, 1] to t = 1, so an ordinary draw is a = πθ (a₀; 0) with a₀ ∼ N (0, I), abbreviated a ∼ πθ ; we overload πθ (a) for the marginal density it induces over clean actions.

At deployment we are given a safe set C ⊆ RD , absent at training, through its Euclidean projection P(a) = arg mina′∈C ∥a′ − a∥, which is closed-form or a cheap iterative solve for the constraints we consider.
Our goal is to draw a ∼ πθ with a ∈ C. We generalize our method to admit continuous cost functions at the end of the section.
Overview.
We want samples that are both safe and plausible.

Rejection sampling and projection are two classical approaches, each achieving one of these: rejection redraws unmodified policy samples until one is safe, so every draw is plausible, but almost all are wasted when safe actions are rare; projection maps the clean sample to the nearest point in the safe set, so every action is safe, but the

<|24|>설정 및 표기법.
<|25|>정책 πθ는 시간 t = 0에서의 가우시안 노이즈 a₀ ∼ N (0, I)로부터 시간 t = 1에서의 깔끔한 행동까지 ODE를 따라 학습된 속도 필드를 적분하여 깔끔한 행동 a ∈ RD를 생성합니다.
<|26|>저희는 시간 t = n ∈ [0, 1]에서의 중간 상태 an으로부터 t = 1까지 적분하는 것을 a = πθ (an; n)으로 표기합니다. 따라서 일반적인 추출은 a₀ ∼ N (0, I)일 때 a = πθ (a₀; 0)이며, 이를 a ∼ πθ로 약칭합니다. 또한 πθ (a)를 깔끔한 행동에 대해 유도되는 주변 밀도(marginal density)로 중복 정의합니다.
<|27|>배포 시점에 저희는 학습 시에는 없었던 안전 집합 C ⊆ RD를 유클리드 투영 P(a) = arg mina′∈C ∥a′ − a∥을 통해 제공받으며, 이는 저희가 고려하는 제약 조건에 대해 닫힌 형식(closed-form)이거나 저렴한 반복적 해결법입니다.
<|28|>저희의 목표는 a ∈ C인 a ∼ πθ를 추출하는 것입니다. 저희는 이 섹션의 마지막에서 연속적인 비용 함수를 허용하도록 방법을 일반화합니다.
<|29|>개요.
<|30|>저희는 안전하면서도 타당한 샘플을 원합니다.
<|31|>기각 샘플링(rejection sampling)과 투영은 두 가지 고전적인 접근 방식이며, 각각 이 중 하나를 달성합니다. 기각 샘플링은 안전한 샘플이 나올 때까지 수정되지 않은 정책 샘플을 다시 추출하므로 모든 추출 결과는 타당하지만, 안전한 행동이 드물 때는 거의 모든 샘플이 낭비됩니다. 투영은 깔끔한 샘플을 안전 집합 내의 가장 가까운 점으로 매핑하므로 모든 행동은 안전하지만,<|end|>
